text:
Ontario Superior Court of Justice

Schwalm (Re)

Date: 2003-01-17

Docket: 31-206765-T

Mr. M. Kestenberg, Ms S. Sack, for
Petitioning Creditor

Mr. A. Birnbaum, for Debtors

Spence J.:

[
1
]

This matter is a bankruptcy petition against the
debtors, William and Judith Schwalm, based on the debtors having failed to meet
their liabilities generally as they come due, pursuant to
S.42
(j) of the
Bankruptcy
and Insolvency Act
R.S.C. 1985, c.B-3 (the "
BIA
" or the
"
Act
").

[
2
]

The debtors, Mr. and Mrs. Schwalm, dispute the
petition on the ground that the conduct of the petitioning creditor, Marker
Canada Limited ("Marker") along with certain other creditors was
designed to force the retail business enterprise of the debtors out of business
in order to prefer the interests of those creditors. The debtors were the
principals in the business known as Old Firehall Sports which was carried on in
Unionville, Ontario. Marker supplies sporting goods to
retailing customers such as the Old Firehall. The other creditors said to have
been seeking to prefer their interests also carry on the sporting goods supply
business to such retail customers.

[
3
]

The debtors say
that all the debts which would otherwise require consideration for purpose of a
bankruptcy determination arise from the failure of the Old Firehall business.
Certain other debts of Mr. Schwalm are said not to be relevant for different
reasons.

[
4
]

The debtors submit
that the conduct of the petitioning creditor, either alone or with the other
creditors, is such that the court should exercise its discretion under
S.43(7)

of the
BIA

not to make a receiving order in bankruptcy against Mrs.
Schwalm and that for other reasons, the Court should make a similar exercise of
its discretion in favour of Mr. Schwalm.

[
5
]

Section 43(7)
of
the
BIA

provides, in the part that is relevant, that "where the
court�c is satisfied by the debtor that he is able to pay his debts, or that
for other sufficient cause no order ought to be made, it shall dismiss the
petition." It is not disputed that the debtors are not able to pay their
debts. The submissions in support of the debtors focus on the conduct of the
petitioning creditor and the related circumstances in the course of events that
led to the petition, and certain other separate considerations mentioned below.
The petitioning creditor disputes the allegations made against it and submits
that the conduct of the debtors militates against their request for the
favourable exercise of the discretion of the court.

Judgments
Based on Claims Relating to The Old Firehall Sports Business

[
6
]

Marker relies on
two judgments which relate to the Old Firehall business. Head/Tyrolia Sports
Canada Inc. obtained judgment against Judith Schwalm (i.e. the debtor, Judy
Schwalm) dated May 1, 2001 for $33,797.85 with interest. No amount has been
paid on the judgment. Marker and three other suppliers, Atomic Sports Canada
("Atomic"), Jupa Sports Inc. ("Jupa") and Skis
Rossignol Canada Ltd. ("Rossignol")
obtained judgment against Mr. &
Mrs. Schwalm dated April 10, 2001 for amounts owing to each of the four companies,
totalling around $270,000 with interest. No amount has been paid on the
Judgment.

[
7
]

The amounts owing are debts that arose from
purchases of goods by the Old Firehall business from the named judgment
creditors. The judgements against the Schwalms are based on guarantees which
they gave for the Old Firehall business debts to those creditors.

The Head/Tyrolia Judgment

[
8
]

The judgment is based on a guarantee which Mrs.
Schwalm gave to Head/Tyrolia in September 1997 for the indebtedness of the Old
Firehall business to Head/Tyrolia.

The Claims of Marker and Related Creditors

[
9
]

Mr. and Mrs. Schwalm gave a guarantee for
liabilities of the Old Firehall business to Jupa on August 17, 1994.

[
10
]

Mr. and Mrs. Schwalm gave guarantees for certain
liabilities of the Old Firehall business owing to Atomic on April 18, 2000.

[
11
]

Mr. and Mrs. Schwalm gave guarantees for
liabilities of the business to Marker on April 3, 2000.

[
12
]

As mentioned below, each of Mr. and Mrs. Schwalm
has other outstanding debts owing to other creditors who were not suppliers of
product to the FireHall business.

Evidence of Mrs. Schwalm in chief

The Background

[
13
]

Mrs. Schwalm became involved in the 1990/91
period with the predecessor business at the same location, which had been
brought out of CCAA protection by a group of creditors. The continuing business
operations ("Firehall I") had initial difficulties in obtaining
supplies of hard goods (i.e. skis and similar and related equipment). The
business did not perform well. The principal creditor, Royal Bank of Canada,
required personal guarantees from the principal shareholders. The business got
lines of credit from its suppliers of hard goods and was able to purchase from
them on normal industry terms. By 1993, the business had become insolvent.
Arrears of retail sales tax were outstanding. A payment arrangement was
negotiated with the provincial authority.

[
14
]

On December 13, 1993, Firehall I filed notice of
intention to make a proposal. By the end of January 1994, the company was
bankrupt. The business closed on February 28, 1994.

[
15
]

Mrs. Schwalm incorporated Firehall Skis and
Sports Inc. ("Firehall II") in January of 1994. She obtained a line
of credit from Benetton. She made arrangements for the supply of hard goods
with Benetton, Rossignol and Head Tyrolia. The business
premises were acquired by Davina Building Corp., a company owned by the Schwalm
Family Trust, with a loan of $400,000 from the trust for the acquisition and
related costs. Additions were made to the building in 1995/96 period with funds
advanced by the trust to Davina under a mortgage held by Mr. Schwalm in trust.

[
16
]

Thus, the new
company carried on the business formerly carried on by Firehall I.

[
17
]

Benetton left the
market in 1997/98 and Marker Canada Inc. assumed the supplying of Marker skis
in 1998. Mrs. Schwalm had dealt with its president, Sean Morris, before, when
he was at Benetton. Morris continued at Marker until October, 2000 when he was
replaced by Mr. Labelle.

[
18
]

In August of 2000
it was announced that Sporting Life, a major retailer in Toronto, was planning
to establish a new store in Markham which would be close to the Firehall
business in Unionville. This news was published against in September.

[
19
]

Mrs. Schwalm was
concerned about the potential new competition and about how to ensure that she
would continue to receive price terms and supply arrangements that would enable
her to remain competitive. She had already, in August, placed her order for
goods with
Rossignol.

[
20
]

Following September, Mrs. Schwalm observed a
change in her business relationship with her suppliers. She began to receive
calls from suppliers pressing her for payment on their outstanding accounts.
This was unusual because at this point in the annual business cycle she was
just at the stage of ordering goods for the next season. Mr. Labelle of Marker
also wanted to know how she was faring in obtaining new financing for the new
business. A similar enquiry was made by Atomic, at the same time.

[
21
]

Mrs. Schwalm found that she had only a limited
supply of hard goods and needed more for the forthcoming Toronto Ski Show in
October, so she made offers to her regular suppliers to purchase for cash up to
$10,000 worth of merchandise. The cash offer was not accepted except by Marker,
which offered $5,000 worth of goods without discount with the balance to be
applied on her outstanding account. She made a deal with Rossignol on terms that were probably not much better.

[
22
]

After the Ski
Show, Mr. Labelle and Mrs. Schwalm had an argument about her outstanding
account with Marker. Mr. Labelle offered only the same cash to goods ratio as
he had proposed earlier in response to further requests from Mrs. Schwalm for
supply of merchandise. In November 2000, Marker made
a de
mand for payment of its outstanding account. Atomic had already made a
demand in respect of its outstanding account.

[
23
]

Mrs. Schwalm consulted a bankruptcy trustee, Jay
Harris. Suppliers called her to enquire about what was going on. She heard that
suppliers were expressing concern over related party transactions in her
company. She expressed her concern that suppliers were trying to put her out of
business to make room for Sporting Life. Mr. Labelle suggested to her there
were suspicions of wrongdoing in her company and said that things were going to
get ugly.

[
24
]

In November of 2000, Firehall II filed a notice
of intention to make a proposal. The period was originally to run to December
27
th
, but was subsequently extended to mid-January 2001. An
extension was then arranged to mid-March 2001. Discussions continued with
suppliers.

[
25
]

Eventually, on March 13
th
or 14
th
,
Mrs. Schwalm and Mr. Schwalm agreed to consent to judgment on their guarantees,
following discussions with Mr. Labelle. Suppliers then asked for a payment of
$25,000, which Mrs. Schwalm did not have. Two groups of suppliers had demands.
The first, consisting of Marker and the others who held personal guarantees,
wanted security for their advances. The other group, consisting of other
members of SICA, the industry credit association, who did not have any
guarantees or other security, wished to participate fully in the security to be
granted to the first group. Specifically, the request was for a first position
on the real estate. Mrs. Schwalm said she was not able to comply with that
request. She offered instead piggy-back rights on the security to be given to
the first group. This issue was never resolved. Neither was the issue Mrs.
Schwalm raised with Marker and the suppliers in its group that she needed
security of supply from them. She understood the piggy-back deal was not
acceptable to the Marker group so she offered a fourth position behind the
Marker group to the SICA group instead. She was told this was not acceptable to
the SICA group. The proposal was defeated at the meeting on March 29, 2001.

[
26
]

From the outset, Mrs. Schwalm sought, with
respect to supply, assurance that the suppliers would make all products
available "with all industry discounts and allowances", which she
considered she needed in order to be able to compete. On March 26, prior to the
meeting, she was advised Marker was not prepared to negotiate all the issues
she had raised. Virtually at the last moment on March 29, Mrs. Schwalm made a
deal with Jupa for its support, which included regular discounts. Atomic
refused to agree to offer industry discounts and allowances on COD purchases by
Firehall. Rossignol's position was the same. The position of Marker was not
clear.

[
27
]

In the proposal period prior to the bankruptcy
of Firehall II, Mrs. Schwalm had obtained product from Marker that was
clear-out product, one or two years old. She did not obtain merchandise from
any of the other suppliers in the Marker group during the proposal period. Just
before the end of the period, Sporting Life announced that it was not going to
proceed with the plan to open in the Markham at that time and said that the
plan was off until 2002.

[
28
]

Mrs. Schwalm believed, from what she understood
about the vote, at the meeting on March 29, 2001 that if either the Marker
group or the SICA group had supported the proposal, it would have had a
possibility of success.

[
29
]

With the defeat of the proposal, the company
went into bankruptcy and the store closed. About two months later in 2001, the
store reopened, still under the Firehall trade name, but now owned and operated
by a company owned by Mrs. Schwalm's son, David
Schwalm. The trade name, according to Mrs. Schwalm, is owned by the Schwalm
Family Trust. Mrs. Schwalm was and is employed as manager of the business.

[
30
]

In the summer of
2001, the new business placed an order with Marker, payable by bank draft or
money order. The order was apparently accepted by Marker but the goods never
arrived. Mrs. Schwalm tried to reach the Vice-President, Sales of Marker, but
without success. She tried some of the other previous suppliers, but did not
get responses. She then sought to make supply arrangements with companies who
had not previously been suppliers to the Firehall business. These deals were
not for product of the quality level that the previous suppliers carried. The
business faxed an order to Elan/Marack, after preliminary discussion, for goods
on a cash or Visa immediate payment basis, and was advised that there was
little product left and it was being saved for existing customers.

[
31
]

Mrs. Schwalm had
tried these two other suppliers without success. She turned to a supplier of
liquidation product and to European sources. She considered that selling only
such product was inadequate for the store to be successful.

[
32
]

At the subsequent
Ski Show in Toronto, Mrs. Schwalm tried to establish relations with suppliers
who had not been involved in the proposal. She had a meeting scheduled with a
representative of Adidas Salomon and she was then told that the company did not
want to open her up, i.e. to sell to her, and she was wasting her time, and she
was refused a meeting. She also tried another supplier, K2 but was told they
would not take an order until their old debt of $15,000 was paid. For the
forthcoming reason, she sourced from European suppliers. Mrs. Schwalm said that
doing so is more expensive, faces limited supply, involves cost differentials
because of currency exchange and is unsatisfactory for ski boots in quantities
desired.

Law

Improper
Purpose; Discretion, etc.

[
33
]

In
Dimples
Diapers Inc. v. Paperboard Industries Corp.,
[1992] O.J. No. 1961
(Ont.
Gen. Div.)
, Farley J. dismissed a bankruptcy petition "solely
because it was brought for an improper purpose" which he said could not be
excised from the bankruptcy proceedings (p. 10 of 14).

[
34
]

Farley J. provided the following analysis (p.9
of 14):

Ordinarily, if it is to the benefit of the
parties that an independent trustee investigate the affairs of a debtor, then a
receiving order should issue: See Re 676915 Ontario Ltd.
(1989), 76 CBR (NS)
164 (Ont. SC)
. However, the Bankruptcy Act
RSC 1985 c.
C-3
has as its purpose the provision of "the orderly and fair distribution
of the property of the bankrupt among its creditors on a pari passu
basis." (Houlden and Morawetz, Bankruptcy law of Canada, 3
rd

ed. p. 1-3). Re De La Hooke
(1934), 15 CBR 485 (Ont.
SC)
held that the petition must not be filed for some
collateral purpose. In that case, the petition was dismissed since it as found
to be filed for the purpose of removing a business competitor who was using a
similar trade name. Houlden and Morawetz went on to say at page 2-45:

When the effect of an agreement between the
petitioning creditor and some non-creditors was to embroil the petitioning
creditor in an improper objective of the purchasers of a business who as
non-creditors had no status in the bankruptcy proceedings and were
intermeddling in it, and the objective was to bring about the bankruptcy of the
debtors, held �\ the whole proceedings was tainted and the Petition must be
dismissed: Re Pappy'
s
Good Eats Ltd.
(1985),
56 CBR (NS) 334

(Ont. Sc)
.

Where a petition is inspired by spite and a
spirit of revenge the court will not grant a receiving order: Re Vipond
(1941),

21 CBR 129
affirmed
22 CBR 268 (Que. CA)
, see Re Westlake
(1984),
53 CBR (NS)
207
(Ont. SC)
.

[
35
]

In
Dallas/North Group Inc., Re,
1999 CanLII 19932 (ON CTGD)
, 46 O.R.
(3d) 602, [1999] O.J. No. 5744 (Ont. Gen. Div.), Ground
J. addressed the same subject as follows (at pages 4 and 5 of 8):

Although I
have found that MMCM has failed to establish either a debt owing to it by the
respondents or acts of bankruptcy by the respondents, I would have dismissed
the petitions even if indebtedness and acts of bankruptcy had been established.

Section 43(7)
of the
Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act, R.S.C. 1985,
c. B.3
as amended (the "BIA") provides that where the court is
satisfied that: "for other sufficient cause no order ought to be
made" it shall dismiss the petition. The case law is clear that the
bankruptcy courts and bankruptcy proceedings should not be used for the purpose
of obtaining some collateral advantage or to settle a dispute between
shareholders and that to purchase a debt for the purpose of bringing a petition
in bankruptcy against the debtor is an improper collateral purpose: see In re
E. DeLaHooke
(1934),
15 C.B.R. 485
; Re Consoli
(1982),
41 C.B.R. (N.S.) 203
(Ont.
S.C.)
; Re Shepard (Receiver of)
(1996)
1996 CanLII 18061 (MB QB)
,
40 C.B.R. (3d) 145
,
109 Man. R.
(2d) 306
(Q.B @.), and
Dimples Diapers Inc. v. Paperboard Industries Corp.
(1992),

15 C.B.R. (3d) 204
(Ont.
Gen. Div.)
.

[
36
]

Ground J. concluded that in that case the
petitions were brought for a collateral purpose and not for the purpose of
obtaining a distribution of the property of the debtors among the creditors.

[
37
]

In
Churchill Forest Industries (Manitoba)
Ltd., Re
(1971),
1971 CanLII 994 (MB QB)
, 23 D.L.R. (3d) 301 (Man. Q.B.), the court said as follows
at p.312:

I come now to the final point ― and
this was strongly urged by counsel for the debtor ― that in any event I
should exercise my discretion under s. 25(7) and dismiss the petition.

The exercise of that discretion must be for
"other sufficient cause" and, as is basic to every exercise of
discretion by the Court, must be founded on sound judicial reasoning arrived at
from the credible evidence adduced, and "must be exercised judicially
according to common sense and justice, and in a manner which does not occasion
a miscarriage of justice": per McFarlane, J.A., in Re Mutual Development
Corp. Ltd. and Approving Officer of the District of Burnaby,
1971 CanLII 981 (BC CA)
, 20 D.L.R. (3d) 505
at p. 508, [1971] 5 W.W.R. 97, quoting for O'Halloran, J.A., in
Poskitt v.
Poskitt and Bishop,
1949 CanLII 221 (BC CA)
, [1949] 3 D.L.R. 798 at p. 812, [1949] 1 W.W.R. 1002.

[
38
]

In
Poskitt v. Poskitt
,
1949 CanLII 221 (BC CA)
, [1949] 3 D.L.R.
798 (B.C. C.A.) the court said, on the subject of discretion but in a context
other than bankruptcy, at p. 812:

A discretion means that at least two proper
judicial decisions are open to the Judge. It does not mean that if he acts
contrary to common sense and justice, that his mere doing so, in itself is an
exercise of discretion. When this happens it is not a mistake in the exercise
of discretion in its proper sense as judicial choice between two judicial
decisions, a defensible exercise of discretion, but it is in truth a failure to
exercise discretion at all. The discretion must be exercised judicially
according to common sense and justice, and in a manner which does not occasion
a miscarriage of justice, and see
Murdoch v. A.-G. B.C.,
1939 CanLII 418 (BC CA)
, [1940] 2 D.L.R.
74 at p. 77, 73 Can. C.C. 222 at pp. 225-6. 54 B.C.R. 496 at p. 501;
Blunt
v. Blunt,
[1943] A.C. 517 at p. 527
and
Taylor v. Vancouver Gen'l
Hospital
(1945),
1945 CanLII 677 (BC CA)
, 62 B.C.R. 79 at p. 80.

[
39
]

In
Kenwood Hills Development Inc., Re,
1995 CanLII 7364 (ON CTGD)
, [1995]
O.J. No. 161 (Ont. Bktcy.) Farley
J. made the following comments at paragraph 10:

I was also
cited Re Benson,
(1936)
18 C.B.R. 99
(Ont.
S.C.)

and Re Dennis,
(1978), 27 c.B.R. (N.S.) 100
(Ont.
S.C.)
as authority for
the proposition that if the debtor has no assets and there is no possibility
that he will have assets in the future, the court should refuse to make a
receiving order. Dennis merely mentioned Benson, but Houlden J.R. relied upon
the fact that a $1000 plus debt had not been proved in refusing the order.
Benson was interesting, in that the female debtor was upwards of 60 years of
age, has no property of any kind, and is at present confined in the
penitentiary. There is no evidence that the debtor is likely to own any
property in the future �c It is admitted that if a receiving order is made
there is no property to vest in the trustee and therefore there is nothing to
administer. (pp.99-100). The petition was dismissed without prejudice. This was
not an auspicious situation for anyone; the bankrupt, the creditor, or the
trustee. I note as well that these were petitions against individuals; the
debtor here is a corporation. Its demise will not prevent anybody from carrying
on their personal or financial lives.

[
40
]

In
Shepard, Re
,

[1996] M.J. No. 203 (Man. Master)
the court said as follows at paragraph 5:

The dominant
purpose of this litigation is not to accomplish the aims and purposes of the

Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act
, but rather to obtain a very important business
advantage. It is not appropriate or indeed, correct in law, to have the courts
facilitate such an objective when the objective is very clearly the main
purpose of the application.

[
41
]

In the Court of
Appeal decision in
Dallas/North Group Inc., Re,
2001 CanLII 3636 (ON CA)
,
[2001] O.J. No. 2743
(Ont. C.A.)

the court said at paragraph 14:

There are special policy considerations to
take into account when dealing with abuse of process in Bankruptcy Court
because bankruptcy proceedings are quasi-criminal in nature and a petition in
bankruptcy can destroy a person's financial standing and reputation.

[
42
]

In
Laserworks Computer Services Inc., Re,
[1997]
N.S.J. No. 564 (N.S. S.C.)
, the court said as follows at paragraph 28 ff:

I can only conclude that the purpose of Datarite
was to effect the bankruptcy of Laserworks. It is a reasonable
supposition that the purpose was to remove a competitor from the marketplace. I
find that it was the intention of Datarite to place
Laserworks into bankruptcy.

I further find that the motive was to
lessen competition.

In my view, Datarite was engaged throughout
in an improper purpose not contemplated by the
B.I.A.
, the purpose of which is
far removed from the use to which Datarite put it.

[
43
]

The court continued as follows at paragraph 41
ff:

It is my opinion that the eighteen
creditors are tainted with the improper motive of Datarite. In Pappy's Good Eats the petition was filed by a creditor with a genuine claim.
The creditor entered into an agreement with three franchisees of the debtor.
This agreement provided that the creditor would prosecute the bankruptcy
proceeding while the franchisees financed the proceeding in exchange for a
share in the dividends. The motive of the franchisees was to bring about a
bankruptcy so as to terminate the franchise agreements between them and the
debtor.

The court
found that there had been an improper use of the bankruptcy legislation. The
effect of the agreement was to embroil the creditor in the improper objectives
of the franchisees who were intermeddling in the proceeding. This tainted the
whole proceeding. Clearly where the object of the intermeddling party is to
bring about the bankruptcy of the debtor an improper purpose is present. The
court will act to prevent such an abuse of the legislation.

The other
cases I have referred to, Dimples Diapers Inc. and Shepard also deal with
bankruptcy petitions instigated for an improper collateral purpose. In Dimples
that purpose was to recover a trademark and a business opportunity. In Shepard
that purpose was to obtain control of certain shares.

[
44
]

In
Hydrofoil
Lake Jet Lines Inc., Re,
[2000] O.J. No. 3181
(Ont.
Bktcy.)

in this
court, Farley J. said at paragraph 16:

What we have here is a debtor that which
does not have any assets or any business. What would the purpose be with
respect to having this company go into bankruptcy? How would that benefit the
creditors of this company? And specifically, we must take into account that the
creditors as a whole, as opposed to just the petitioning creditors. (sic)

[
45
]

Farley J. continued as follows at paragraph 18:

Clearly on that scenario there may be an
advantage for the Tischenko Group that they shut down the debtor in a
bankruptcy. It might even be better for Mr. Makarchuk. But it certainly would
not provide any advantage to the creditors, outside of the petitioning
creditors and Mr. Makarchuk, to have a bankruptcy.

[
46
]

Farley J. concluded as follows at paragraph 20:

In my view the evidence in this trial is
overwhelming. The petitions were brought for a collateral purpose and not for
the purpose of obtaining a distribution of the property of the respondents
among their creditors and not for an appropriate bankruptcy related
investigation. Now while there is no purchase of a debt, certainly it appears
that the collateral advantage here was to eliminate the debtor, and
particularly the debtor with the shareholders that it had not worked out with
the Tischenko interests and I Mr. Makarchuk. To remove in effect Mr. Makarchuk
from the scene is a collateral purpose which is improper and, for the reason
alone, I dismiss the petition

Duress

[
47
]

The headnote to the report of the decision of
the Court of Appeal in
Gordon v. Roebuck
(1992),
1992 CanLII 7443 (ON CA)
, 9 O.R. (3d) 1 (Ont.
C.A.), provides the following instructive summary:

To succeed in
the main action,
G
had to show economic duress and also
that the coercion exerted was illegitimate. The four factors to consider in
determining whether a party's will has been coerced were proven. First, there
was evidence of protest by G's agent. Second, there was no realistic
alternative under the circumstances since court proceedings were not practical
given the complexity of the matter and the immediacy of the closing of the
transaction. Third although
G
had independent legal advice, under
the circumstances the advice likely would have been to capitulate to the
demands of the party exercising the pressure. Fourth,
G
took steps to avoid the contract within a reasonable time. The trial
judge was wrong in concluding that there was no economic duress. However, that
did not end the matter because the onus was
on G to
show also that the coercion exerted was illegitimate. The trial judge was
entitled to hold that G had not satisfied that onus.

[
48
]

A helpful discussion of the legal concept of
duress in the context of business dealings is set out in Waddams,
The Law of
Contracts,
3
rd
ed. (Canada Law Book, 1993) at para. 504 to 506,
as follows:

Recent cases have openly recognized
economic duress as a defence. In
Occidental Worldwide Investment Corp. v.
Skibs
A/S Avanti (The "Siboen" and The
"Sibotre")
and in
The Atlantic Baron,
it
was held that economic coercion would amount to duress. These cases were
approved by the Privy Council in
Pao On v. Lau Yiu Long
on the basis
that the pressure amounted to "a coercion of will which vitiates
consent". The Board indicated factors relevant to making the necessary
determination:

In determining
whether there was a coercion of will such that there was no true consent, it is
material to inquire whether the person alleged to have been coerced did or did
not protest; whether, at the time he was allegedly coerced into making the
contract, he did or did not have an alternative course open to him such as an
adequate legal remedy; whether he was independently advised; and whether after
entering the contract he took steps to avoid it.

The case itself held that an agreement made
under threat of breach of a preexisting contract was enforceable. On the facts
it was a realistic and practicable option for the promisor to refuse to make
the second agreement; the inconvenience of resorting to a legal remedy was not,
in itself, proof of duress.

In some cases, of which
Pao On
is an
example, a benefit is secured by a threat to break a pre-existing contract. A
supplier, for example, having promised to deliver at certain price, may
subsequently demand a higher price. If at the time of the demand, alternate
sources of supply have disappeared and the recipient is in urgent need of the
supply, there is an element of economic duress. In cases where the agreement to
pay the higher price is still executory, many courts have refused enforcement
on the basis that there is absence of consideration.

As suggested in an earlier chapter, this is
hardly a satisfactory ground for relief and it will be ineffective if the
recipient has given some value (however small), has executed a promise under
seal, or has actually complied with the supplier's demand by making payment. A
sounder ground for relief is economic duress, which has now been adopted in
recent cases. It is not easy, however, to say precisely what is not a
satisfactory criterion. Nor is the wrongfulness of the promisee's conduct, for
relief has been given where there is now wrongful conduct, and it is in any
case doubtful whether an invitation to renegotiate a contract is
"wrongful". The reasonableness of the terms is not whether those
terms standing alone are reasonable, but whether the promisor should be bound
by a promise to abandon something the promisor then possesses,
viz,
valuable
rights under a former enforceable contract. In the end it seems that no better
test can be found than the general test of unconscionability, that is, whether
the promisee has taken undue advantage of inequality of bargaining power. The
degree to which the promisor has, as a practical matter, alternative courses of
action will be a weighty factor in assessing whether there is inequality of
bargaining power.

Analysis of the Issues

The Purposes of the Petitioner

[
49
]

The debtors say that the petitioner bring this
petition for improper purposes. Essentially they say the petitioner wishes to
prevent Mrs. Schwalm from re-entering the sporting goods retail business
because of their unsatisfactory experience with her in their business dealings
leading up to the bankruptcy.

[
50
]

Some questions about this submission may be
identified here is a preliminary way. Why would the petitioner go to the
considerable expense of prosecuting this bankruptcy petition if that were its
concern and its objective? The Firehall business has been resumed with Mrs.
Schwalm's son David indicated to be the owner and Mrs.
Schwalm the general manager. It does not seem that the petitioner is dealing
with Firehall. There is no evidence that it is under any obligation to do so.
So it is not apparent how a bankruptcy can affect its position vis-à-vis
having to deal with Mrs. Schwalm. As for Mrs. Schwalm, it is
not apparent that if she were bankrupt, that would prevent from being employed
as general manager in David Schwalm's store, so a
bankruptcy would not significantly further the objective of keeping Mrs.
Schwalm out of the business generally.

[
51
]

It was submitted
that the petitioner and the other suppliers did not like dealing with Mrs.
Schwalm for unworthy reasons which were unrelated to business concerns. This
submission is dealt with elsewhere in these reasons. Even if the submission
were substantiated that would still not give the petitioner an adequate motive
to seek a bankruptcy order against Mrs. Schwalm, now that her company is no
longer operating. In any event, the submission is not well-founded, for the
reasons set out below.

[
52
]

A related
submission was that the petitioner and other suppliers were engaging in practices
contrary to the competition law. This is dealt with elsewhere on these reasons.
The submission was employed in a related contention, i.e. that Mrs. Schwalm
showed an intention not to comply with certain of the anti-competitive
practices required of her and this was a factor in the suppliers' dislike for
dealing with her. It is prima facie plausible as a general matter that a
supplier could seek to bankrupt an ungovernable retailer as a means of
disciplining retailers, so the submission deserves further consideration. It is
dealt with below.

[
53
]

It was submitted
that the petitioner and the other suppliers, for the reasons mentioned above,
did not wish to do business with Mrs. Schwalm but were content to do so until
the prospect of the new Sporting Life outlet emerged and they then acted in
concert to close down her business. This submission is dealt with further
below. Why this motivation would also prompt an effort to put Mrs. Schwalm
personally into bankruptcy is not apparent. In any event, the submission is not
well-founded, for the reasons set out below.

[
54
]

The petitioner
says that its concern throughout in its dealings with Mrs. Schwalm in respect
of the Firehall business was to obtain reliable arrangements for timely payment
of outstanding accounts and that it is engaged in this petition for the purpose
of ensuring that all assets that belong to the debtors are discovered so that
they can be made available to meet the proper claims of the creditors. Some
preliminary comment here is also in order.

[
55
]

As noted elsewhere
in these reasons, the debtors have dealt with a number of assets in a way that
the petitioner says raises questions that can most appropriately be pursued
through the procedures a bankruptcy would make available. The petitioner says
this is also the case in respect of the Schwalm Family Trust. Prima facie it
would seem that if the debtors have an interest in the Schwalm Family Trust or
its assets, that interest would be available as part of the bankruptcy estate.
If the Schwalm Family Trust is not a validly constituted trust or if some of
the assets purportedly owned by it are not its own but rather belong to the
Schwalms, then the estate would be in a position to recover these assets. It
might be that the doctrine of constructive trust would apply in respect of some
of the dealings of the Schwalms or the Firehall company with the Family Trust,
such that some part of its assets could be determined to be subject to a
constructive trust ultimately in favour of the estate. Whether these possible
outcomes can be established is not determinable at present.

[
56
]

It was submitted
that a bankruptcy of the debtors would be useless for the creditors because any
assets that might be recovered would be subject to the security that the Family
Trust holds over assets of the Firehall company. Prima facie, this would seem to
be correct to the extent that those assets belong to the Firehall company and
the Family Trust security on those assets is a valid one. But those questions
are not foreclosed. Moreover, they do not necessarily affect the question
whether the Trust is itself a valid trust and whether, either because of some
invalidity in the Trust or otherwise, the debtors have an interest in the
assets held by the Trust.

[
57
]

The preliminary
comment on these matters relating to the Family Trust is that they cannot be
resolved at the present time because of the limited information available about
the Trust and the bankruptcy process is one that is well-suited for the purpose
of resolving such issues as these.

Hostility
towards Mrs. Schwalm

[
58
]

It is argued that
the suppliers wanted rid of Mrs. Schwalm because they considered her to be
unacceptably different from the people they dealt with and wished to deal with.
It was suggested that it was factor working against her that Mrs. Schwalm is a
woman and most of the people on the suppliers' side are men. However, not all
of them are; Ms. Beamish of
Amer/
Atomic gave evidence for the
petitioner. There was no evidence that the suppliers had a reluctance to deal
with Mrs. Schwalm and wanted to terminate their dealings with her because she
is a woman.

[
59
]

In the submission on this issue of Mrs. Schwalm's
difference counsel also referred to the fact that Mrs. Schwalm
is Jewish as if to invite, with expressly saying so, that it was the fact of
her being Jewish that made Mrs. Schwalm unacceptable to the suppliers. Mrs.
Schwalm gave evidence about remarks that Mr. Labelle of Marker made to her
which she took to be anti-semitic. One of the remarks was to the effect that
the Italian and German participants in the direction of the Marker business
would not find Mrs. Schwalm's plans acceptable. There
is no reason to doubt that Mrs. Schwalm sincerely construed this remark to be
directed at her as an anti-semitic comment. However, there is no reason to
conclude that Mr. Labelle intended the remark to carry that implication.

[
60
]

What is clear from the evidence is that Marker
and a number of the other suppliers had continuing and mounting concerns over
the Firehall's business practices relating to sales inventory and payment to
the suppliers. Specifically, the concern was that Mrs. Schwalm was employing
the arrangements that suppliers afforded to her and other retailers to defer
payment in respect of unsold inventory (referred to as "redating") to
appropriate to the use of her business the proceeds of inventory sales without
paying the suppliers out of those proceeds. It was this concern and their lack
of confidence that Mrs. Schwalm would alter her practice, as they saw it, that
led them to consider that she had ceased to be acceptable as a retailer. This
was not an unreasonable concern on their part. As a matter of commercial
judgment, it was not unreasonable for them to come to the conclusion that Mrs.
Schwalm was not a person with whom one could reliably do business.

The Development of the Business Crisis and
the Prospect of Sporting Life

[
61
]

The prospect of a new Sporting Life outlet being
opened in Markham was first announced in August of 2000 and the news about it
was published again in September. Mrs. Schwalm said she observed a change in
her business relationship with her suppliers in that month. In November of
2000, Firehall II filed its notice of intention to make a proposal. The
proposal period lasted until the end of March 2001. Prior to the end of the
proposal period, Sporting Life announced it was not going to proceed with the
plan to open in Markham. Firehall II went into bankruptcy when the proposal
failed. The petition against the debtors was initiated sometime later.

[
62
]

Representatives of the petitioner and other
suppliers gave evidence about their developing concerns about their outstanding
accounts with Firehall II.

[
63
]

Mr. Labelle of Marker said that at a meeting in
January 2000 with SICA representatives there was a discussion with Mrs. Schwalm
about her cash flow problems. He communicated with Mrs. Schwalm in February of
2000 requiring guarantees, a fixed charge and a reduction in the account in
February 2000. The guarantees were provided in April. These events antedated
the announcement of the Sporting Life plan by some months. There was no
evidence to suggest that Marker was not in earnest when it asserted in February
2000 its conditions for credit for the next winter.

[
64
]

Mr. Labelle said
that there were probably no more shipments to Firehall after the February 28
meeting, despite requests for goods from Mrs Schwalm. Prior to that, he said,
some shipments were made for cash on the basis that for each $1.50 paid, $1.00
was applied to the order and the balance to the outstanding account. Marker
received no further payments from Firehall II until some late payments were
made during the proposal period when Marker made some shipments on a cash
basis. It did not receive the fixed charge it said it required. The fact that
it was not prepared, in the fall season that followed, to extend credit in the
manner it had done in the past cannot be regarded as a novel or surprising
development in view of the February letter.

[
65
]

Mr. Labelle said
that at the time of the February letter Firehall II owed Marker $112,000. For
that winter season he said that a significant quantity of goods had been
shipped to Firehall based on orders placed in August and September of 1999 on
terms calling for payment in December and January and that by January only 30%
of the goods supplied were still on hand at the store but payments had not been
received by Marker.

[
66
]

Subsequently in
November, 2000 he discovered at the Firehall premises that the goods Marker had
shipped had been sold but not paid for. He next learned from a SICA meeting
that Atomic had issued a demand notice to Firehall and he decided that Marker
would do the same.

[
67
]

Mr. Labelle
recalled that Sporting Life had announced its plan to open in the Unionville
area but he said he did not recall when the announcement was made or who told
him about it.

[
68
]

With respect to
the November 2000 discovery that Firehall had no Marker inventory at a time
when the outstanding account was still $100,000, Mr. Labelle said this could
only mean that the proceeds of the sale of the Marker goods had been applied
either to pay other suppliers or to finance losses but in either case it was
bad news for Marker and it was a concern to be asked by Firehall in those
circumstances to ship more goods to it.

[
69
]

In view of the
evidence, it must be concluded that at least from January 2000 Marker was
concerned about the unpaid account of Firehall and by February had decided to
take action about it by requiring security and repayments and not shipping on
credit until it was satisfied that Firehall had achieved a reliable condition, which
never happened. Thus the dynamic that operated in the fall of 2000 was
effectively initiated early in that year. The evidence does not show that the
position of Marker towards Firehall hardened after the announcement of the
Sporting Life proposal. The business relationship between Firehall and Marker
was already off the rails at that point and the troubles of the fall of 2000
simply brought to realization the breach in the relationship that had occurred
many months before and had not been overcome in the intervening period.

[
70
]

Ms. Beamish, a
representative of
Amer
Sports Canada Inc. (of which Atomic is
a division), another supplier and a member of SICA, said she wrote to Firehall
on April 5, 2000 to set out a requirement for payments to be made in the following
December, which were not made. In January, 2000 a Firehall cheque to
Amer
had been "pay-stopped" and Mrs. Schwalm had refused or failed
to take a call from Ms. Beamish about the account. Ms. Beamish said it was
becoming apparent she couldn't trust Mrs. Schwalm. Ms. Beamish said it would
have been a detriment to
Amer
if Mrs. Schwalm were to be put out of
business because it would result in lost revenue.

[
71
]

The evidence of Mrs. Schwalm does not provide
any basis for a different view of the development of the Firehall's business crisis. It started well before the Sporting Life
announcement, because of supplier concerns about the outstanding accounts owed
by Firehall. The evidence does not suggest that the Sporting Life prospect was
a significant factor in the dealings between Marker and the other suppliers and
Firehall.

[
72
]

By the early part
of 2000, the suppliers were no longer prepared to put up with the payment
problems they were experiencing with Firehall. The situation did not improve
during the first half of 2000. The demands for payment arose out of these
circumstances and not the Sporting Life prospect. The resulting legal
proceedings continued after the Sporting Life prospect was deferred, which is
consistent with that prospect not having been a significant factor in the
actions taken by Marker and the other suppliers.

The
Guarantees and the Consent to Judgment

[
73
]

Mrs. Schwalm said
that, during the proposal period, there was discussion back and forth on
whether there would be a consent to judgment. It was finally agreed in
mid-March that there would be a postponement in respect of the proposal steps,
ie. an extension of time in favour of the business, provided Mrs. Schwalm would
consent to judgment. She said Mr. Labelle said things were going to get ugly
otherwise and she was disturbed by this and consented to judgment. She said she
consented to judgment with the other creditors because she believed they were
acting in unison and that Mr. Labelle spoke for them.

[
74
]

Earlier, when she
had been asked for the guarantees, she said was not asked for a net worth
statement or personal financial statement and none was provided.

[
75
]

Mrs. Schwalm said
the action on the guarantee was started prior to the scheduling of the first
meeting with creditors in respect of the proposal but subsequent to the filing
of the notice of intention.

[
76
]

She said that when
she was asked to sign the consent to judgment, she didn't want to do so and
wanted an opportunity to negotiate with suppliers to resolve the problems of
Firehall. She was upset that the creditors were acting on the consent. She said
she believed they misused the guarantee, in that she was making headway with
payables and she did not feel that the debt was due, in view of the manner of
dealing between Firehall and the creditors over the past seven years and the
fact that the business was now recovering.

[
77
]

She said that when
she signed the consent to judgment the situation was that otherwise the
business would fail, without any opportunity for survival.

[
78
]

Mrs. Schwalm said
that it was only after she signed the consent to judgment that Mr. Labelle told
her that Marker needed a payment of $25,000.

[
79
]

Mr. Schwalm said
he signed the guarantee in favour of Marker because Sean Morris of Marker asked
him to and said it was necessary and Mrs. Schwalm was signing a guarantee.
Morris did not ask Mr. Schwalm for a net worth statement. Mr. Schwalm said
Morris did not know about his personal financial affairs. He signed other
guarantees for the Firehall business when Mrs. Schwalm asked him to. He had
independent legal advice for only one of the guarantees. He said he was not
asked for a net worth statement about his financial circumstances.

[
80
]

Mr. Labelle of
Marker said that at about the time of a meeting in January of 2000 with SICA
representatives and Mrs. Schwalm about her cash flow problems, he saw a form of
guarantee that Mrs. Schwalm had provided earlier to Marker. In February he told
Mr. and Mrs. Schwalm that guarantees in a new form would be required for credit
for winter 2000/2001.
Mr. Labelle's
evidence was that he wanted a
guarantee from Mr. Schwalm because he understood he had an interest in the
business. His letter to the Schwalms dated February 28, 2000 said that if all
of the requirements in that letter were met (i.e., balance of outstanding
account not to exceed $50,000 as at April 20, 2000; unlimited fixed charge on
170 Main Street, Unionville in form acceptable to Marker, and the two
guarantees), Marker envisioned that credit would be available to Firehall on
the terms set out in the letter. At that time, Marker was not shipping new
goods to Firehall without receiving concurrent payment. He said the guarantee
was not executed for several months. The guarantees were sent in executed form
dated April 3, 2000 to Marker under a letter of that date.

[
81
]

The fixed charge contemplated by the letter was
never given. It was not stated or submitted that the limitation on the
outstanding balance as at April 1, 2000 was satisfied. The last payment for
goods Marker received from Firehall prior to the proposal period was in
February, 2000. Mr. Labelle said that his plan in setting out the three
requirements in February 2000 was that if they were satisfied that would
protect the receivable owing to Marker from Firehall. He said he did not make
enquiries of the other suppliers in the winter of 2000 about what credit
information and/or guarantees they had in respect of Firehall. His sole motive
was to protect the position of Marker and its ability to collect efficiently.

[
82
]

He said that months later, in November, when
Mrs. Schwalm had not fulfilled any of her goals and Atomic was about to take
legal proceedings on its account, he did not see that he had a choice not to
cooperate with the other suppliers. He had no prospect of getting a better
security position and Mrs. Schwalm was in danger of facing the winter 2000/2001
season without money for new product. Mr. Labelle said that during the proposal
period in March of 2001 he took the position, as did other suppliers, that if
the Schwalms would not consent to judgment on the guarantee, he would proceed
to obtain judgment and would stop trying to help with respect to the proposal.
He said that if agreement was not possible on the amount owing, it would not be
possible on anything else.

Anti-Competitive Practices

[
83
]

The debtors say that Marker engaged in practices
that violate the
Competition Act
.
They refer to
s.50
of the
Act

relating
to illegal trade practices,
s.52(1)
as to false and misleading representations,

s.61(1)
the prohibition as resale price maintenance,
s.61(3)
, the prohibition
on suggested retail price,
s.61(6)
on refusal to supply and to provisions
relating to refusal to deal.

[
84
]

The debtors submit that the practice which
Marker followed, of supplying a price list with a legend "minimum
advertised price", was contrary to the
Competition Act
.
There is no
evidence of any complaints to or from the competition law authorities. It was
not shown that the advertising practices caused any problem in the dealings
between the Firehall and Marker. There is no basis for an inference that Marker
sought to discipline Firehall for a failure or reluctance on its part to
comply.

[
85
]

The debtors submit that the petitioner refused
to allow and to grant discounts and allowances to Firehall contrary to the
Competition
Act
.
The provisions of the
Act

in this regard do not create offences
as such but only practices that are reviewable and may be subject to the making
of an order.

[
86
]

There is evidence that in March 2001 Marker took
the position that the terms of sale to Firehall would be cash before delivery,
no standard discounts and no standard allowances. The debtors say this refusal was
contrary to the
Act

or at least demonstrated bad faith.

[
87
]

There was evidence that other suppliers also
refused to offer standard discounts and allowance to Firehall, and that without
their discounts and allowances, Firehall could not be competitive.

[
88
]

The petitioner responds that the reason for its
unwillingness to deal with Mrs. Schwalm on the standard basis was it was not
prepared to offer favourable credit terms and prices without receiving payment
as goods were sold. The evidence supports their characterization. There is no
evidence Firehall ever complained to Marker or to the authorities that its
conduct violated the
Competition Act
.

[
89
]

Whether or not the conduct of the petitioner or
any of the other suppliers failed to comply with the
Competition Act

in
respect of the matters mentioned above, that conduct cannot be regarded in its
context as being so reprehensible as regards Mrs. Schwalm as to be a basis for
refusing to grant the petition.

Quasi-Partnership

[
90
]

The debtors submit that the business
relationship between Marker and Firehall was such that they should be
considered "stakeholders" or "quasi-partners" in the ski
industry. The terms "stakeholder" and "quasi-partner" do
not describe a recognized legal status. It is argued that the business
relationship that had developed over years between the two enterprises was such
that Marker could not act towards Firehall in such a way that its business
would fail, unless it was seeking to obtain the payment of debts. Marker's
position is that that, in effect, is what it was trying to do. In any event the
argument for a status of "quasi-partner" with some vague
responsibility with fiduciary characteristics disregards the fact that unlike a
partnership, the relationship of supplier and customer involves interests that
are fundamentally different rather than common. Partners are entitled to share
directly in the division of the same proceeds. A supplier must look to the
customer for payment by the customer.

Duress

[
91
]

The debtors submit that, by reason of duress the
guarantees given in 2000 might very well have been determined to be
unenforceable if that issue had been litigated, and the court should consider
this factor in determining whether to exercise its discretion. The argument is
that by the time the guarantees were sought in 2000, the Firehall business had
become economically dependent on supply from Marker and the guarantees were
required as a condition of further supply on credit which was in fact never
forthcoming.

[
92
]

The debtors advance as a related consideration
that none of the suppliers who asked for and obtained their guarantees asked
for a net worth statement of the debtors or other information about their
financial position. It is not apparent why anything should be thought to turn
on this point. It was not suggested that a supplier cannot properly take a
guarantee without making such enquiries. In such circumstances the guarantee
would simply be of unknown value, but no reason is given to consider the taking
of such a guarantee to be objectionable. There was a suggestion that without
making a request for a net worth statement the recipients could not be
considered to have relied on the guarantees, but that is not persuasive. All
that reasonably could be said is that the recipient of the guarantee wanted the
guarantee for whatever it is worth and ought to be presumed to be relying on it
on that basis.

[
93
]

Indeed Mrs. Schwalm in her letter of April 3,
2002 to Marker invited Marker to rely on the guarantees, in the following
terms:

The intent of the guarantee is in the event
of failure of the business known as Firehall Skis & Sports Inc.,
you
would have the ability to recover any amounts owing to you from Bill and I
personally
. As I understand both of our intentions are to be supportive of
each other and continuing doing business as in the past. (emphasis added)

[
94
]

There is no suggestion that there was any formal
defect in the guarantees that would render them invalid. The Marker
requirements for the guarantees plus the account reduction and the fixed charge
had been communicated to Mrs. Schwalm. Marker did not suggest to the Schwalms
that by reason of the guarantees being received, it was prepared to discard its
other two requirements.

[
95
]

The question that was not raised specifically,
but could be, is this: if Marker was not prepared to rely on the guarantees by
themselves to restore the supply of goods on credit, should it be able to rely
on the guarantees to assert a claim under them? Marker already had guarantees
from the Schwalms and it is not evident that they were defective. This point
favours Marker: it was not changing the business deal with the Schwalms by
asking for and obtaining the new guarantees.

[
96
]

Moreover, the Schwalms gave their consent to
judgment on the guarantees. It is submitted for the debtors that the consent
was obtained by duress of a kind that, even if not sufficient to meet the test
to set aside the judgments, constitutes a factor to be taken into account with
respect to the exercise of the discretion of the Court.

[
97
]

One factor that is said to be an element in the
duress is that the action on the guarantee was commenced after the notice of
intent to make the proposal was filed. It is not suggested that commencing the
action at that time was a breach of the law or of any understanding between
Marker and the Schwalms. If it was not, it is hard to see why the unilateral
act of Firehall in giving notice of its intention to make a proposal should
disable beneficiaries of the Schwalms as guarantors from taking action as their
guarantees.

[
98
]

It is also submitted for the Schwalms that all
that they received in return for their consent to judgment was agreement by the
creditors to adjourn the date for their meeting for two weeks. This is so. But
obtaining an adjournment in such circumstances is, for the debtor, a way of
obtaining more time to try to make a deal with the creditors. It is not
suggested that the extension of time was made inconsequential by some action or
failure to act on the part of the petitioner.

[
99
]

With respect to the criteria of economic duress,
as set out in the
Pao On v. Lau Yiu Long
case [
Pao On v. Lau Yiu Long

(1979), [1980] A.C. 614 (Hong Kong P.C.)
] cited in the extract from
Waddams
on the Law of Contracts
above, in the present case the Schwalm did not
protest, they were independently advised and they took no steps to avoid the
bargain they made In effect, they gave their consent to obtain the extension of
time and they obtained the extension as a result; now that, after the fact, the
extension has proved useless to them, the Schwalms seek to challenge the
validity of the consent. The fact that the Schwalms had counsel is also
relevant. They wanted the adjournment, they could reasonably consider it be
worth paying the price of the consent to judgment. It is not shown, as is
required for a determination of unconscionability in a case of unequal
bargaining power, that Marker in effect importuned the Schwalms into the
bargain of a consent to a judgment in return for the extension, and it is not
shown that that bargain was improvident.

[
100
]

So the circumstances of the obtaining of the consent to judgment do
not disclose any objectionable feature that would provide a basis for an
exercise of the court's discretion in favour of the debtors and against the
petition.

Conclusion as to Improper Purpose

[
101
]

For the above reasons, it is not shown that the petitioner is acting
on the basis of an improper purpose in pursuing the petition.

No Adequate Purpose would be served by
Bankruptcy

[
102
]

It was submitted for the debtors that, having regard to all the
circumstances, no adequate purpose would be served by granting the petition for
a receiving order against them. The extent to which such a principle provides a
proper ground for the exercise of the discretion of the court is best approached
in terms of the particular circumstances and issues raised.

[
103
]

The position of the debtors is that there is very little to be
gained for the creditors by a bankruptcy and that the bankruptcy will have
detrimental consequences for the debtors that will not be justified by any
prospects of deriving further benefits through the bankruptcy process. The
petitioner disputes this characterization of the situation.

[
104
]

With respect to the detriment to the debtors, it is apparent that
bankruptcy may well carry some detrimental consequences. Mrs. Schwalm said that
she might well be able to obtain credit while carrying an undischarged judgment
because she would have an opportunity to explain it to prospective credit
providers, but that would not be the case if she were bankrupt. To the extent
that that is so, it does not seem to be an inappropriate consequence of
bankruptcy as a general matter. No reason is advanced why, if Mrs. Schwalm is
otherwise a person who is properly to be determined to be bankrupt, she should
not be subject to the consequences that flow from bankruptcy.

[
105
]

There was evidence that Mr. Schwalm is in poor health. Bankruptcy
would be an additional burden. He said that bankruptcy would also be
potentially damaging to him in respect of the charitable work that he
undertakes.

[
106
]

Considerations of this kind by themselves do not assist in
determining how the discretion of the court should be exercised. For that
purpose, the focus should instead be on another submission of the debtors, which
is that no adequate purpose would be served by a bankruptcy. In this regard,
the debtors raise the issues considered below.

Section 163 of the
Bankruptcy Act

[
107
]

It was submitted that Mr. Labelle of Marker knew or could be taken
to know that if the inspectors of Firehall had concerns about the Family Trust
they could have required an examination under s.163 of the
Bankruptcy Act.
That
this step was not taken is said to be suspicious particularly when there had
not been a judgment debtor examination of Mr. Schwalm, who provided a doctor's
letter to explain his non-attendance for examination. This latter point is not
persuasive: there is nothing to show that Marker ought to have considered Mr.
Schwalm's indisposition on the day in question to be other than
convenient.

[
108
]

The debtors say
that the Firehall creditors could still proceed with a section 163 examination,
or seek the appointment of an equitable receiver or seek the appointment of a
receiver in aid of execution.

[
109
]

The point that is
sought to be advanced by reference to s.163 and the other possible remedies is,
or seems to be, that since Marker, as a creditor of Firehall, did not join with
the other creditors of Firehall to pursue all possible courses of action open to
them before the creditors with guarantees decided to resort to their guarantees
and Marker decided to petition based on its guarantee, this failure to resort
to other remedies first should lead to an inference of bad faith on the part of
Marker in proceeding as it has done and an inference that bankruptcy of the
Schwalms would serve no adequate purpose. There is no evidence to assist in
respect of the hypothesis of bad faith. It is at least equally credible that
Marker, based on its dealings with the Schwalms, concluded that the only way
they could reliably obtain and act upon conclusive information about the role
of the Family Trust was by proceeding with a petition against the Schwalms.

[
110
]

No effort has been
made by the debtors to show that all relevant information relating to the
Family Trust would reliably be made available in the Firehall bankruptcy.
Indeed from the evidence of Mrs. Schwalm the proper inference is that, in view
of the involvement of Mrs. Schwalm and Mr. Schwalm in dealings with the Family
Trust that related, or may have related, to Firehall, the bankruptcy of the
Schwalms, if otherwise warranted, would most likely be the most effective way
to secure the relevant information about the Family Trust.

No benefit to
creditors

[
111
]

The debtors submit
that they have no material assets or income, so a bankruptcy would not help the
creditors. There is
prime facie
evidence that the debtors have no
material assets or income but the matter is made problematic by the dealings
that have occurred with the Family Trust and with the real estate interests in
two condos and the family home that have been owned by or for the benefit of
and have been enjoyed by the Schwalm family.

[
112
]

For the debtors it
is said that, in the Firehall bankruptcy, the Trustee in Bankruptcy, Mr. Harris
advised that he had not found any reviewable transactions and that there was
also an opinion given by a lawyer, Mr.
Manis
, that the
Family Trust held valid security on the assets of Firehall, and that Mrs.
Schwalm in her evidence had responded satisfactorily to the questions put to
her about the Family Trust dealings. On this basis it was submitted that there
was no basis for concern that would support further enquiry about the Family
Trust and that there was no prospective benefit to the creditors in any event
because the Family Trust's valid security over the assets of Firehall means
that the creditors of Firehall are necessarily subordinate to that security.

[
113
]

The latter
argument begs the question. In principle if the dealings with the Family Trust
are open to challenge by the creditors of the Schwalms the fact that the
security held by the Family Trust was apparently valid as regards Firehall will
not necessarily and will not likely stand in the way of efforts by the
creditors of the Schwalms to advance their claims against the Family Trust
through the bankruptcy of the Schwalms. Nor should the creditors of the
Schwalms, or this court, necessarily be bound by the view formed by the Trustee
in Bankruptcy. On a bankruptcy, a trustee does what it can in such
circumstances but the creditors may still consider a prospective claim to be
worth pursuing where the trustee does not.

[
114
]

So the real issue
here is the contention advanced on behalf of the debtors that there is simply
no reason to make further enquiry about the dealings of the debtors and in
particular in respect of the dealings with the Family Trust.

Dealings by
the Schwalms

[
115
]

Mr. and Mrs.
Schwalm were the trustees of the Schwalm Family Trust, a trust established for
the benefit of their family, until shortly before the hearing of the petition,
when they resigned their trustee positions in favour of a friend of theirs.
They said they resigned on the advice of their lawyer. No other explanation was
offered to the court for their resignation. In the absence of any substantive
reason, the resignation of the Schwalms from the trusteeship of a trust for
their own family, in favour of a person who is not a member of the family, is a
cause for suspicion.

[
116
]

When Mrs. Schwalm
provided to Marker the guarantees from Mr. Schwalm and herself for Firehall,
she advised Marker that the purpose of the guarantees was to provide assurance
that Marker would be paid. Firehall prepared financial statements for at least
some of the years in question, and the financial statements disclosed that
there were shareholders' advances outstanding. However, the financial
statements did not disclose that this item referred to obligations to the
Schwalm Family Trust for which the Trust held security over the assets of
Firehall.

[
117
]

In her testimony
Mrs. Schwalm said, in connection with the Firehall business, that she used the
Family Trust as a kind of "clearing house". She paid money into it
and withdrew money from it. What this meant was not clarified further. The
impression is left that the Trust simply functioned as the
alter ego
of
Mrs. Schwalm. According to Mrs. Schwalm, Firehall had debt obligations to the
Family Trust in connection with the financing of the purchase and renovation of
the Firehall premises, but even if that is so, it does not explain the nature
of her financial dealings with the Trust in respect of the ongoing Firehall
business or allow any assessment to be made of whether she has any interest in
or claim against the Trust that would potentially benefit the creditors. All
that can be concluded is that the Schwalms' dealings with the Trust in respect
of the Firehall business may well have resulted in the Trust having received
assets which Firehall or Mr. Schwalm or Mrs. Schwalm might otherwise have
received and enjoyed. That is not a reason that militates against a receiving
order. It is, on the contrary, a factor that supports a receiving order, as a
way to allow the fullest possible investigation to be made of the affairs of
the debtors in circumstances such as are present here, where there are
questions for which answers are not provided or otherwise foreseeable. Based on
the conduct of the Schwalms to date and the evidence given at the hearing there
is no reason to consider that these matters can be properly resolved without
employing the procedures which the bankruptcy law is designed to make
available.

[
118
]

Based on the above
analysis, a bankruptcy here would serve an adequate and proper purpose. In addition,
it is appropriate to note that there have been other transactions which raise
questions as to whether they may have had the effect or intended effect of
putting assets out of the reach of creditors.

[
119
]

A 21 per cent interest in the
matrimonial home was sold to the daughters of the Schwalms the day after the
Firehall proposal was voted down. A condo or timeshare unit at
Mont Tremblant
was owned by Davina Financial, a company owned by
the Family Trust. A condo in Boca Raton was owned, according to Mr. Schwalm, in
trust for his children. It was sold in the last year or so. Mr. Schwalm said
the proceeds were ultimately paid to Mrs. Schwalm'
s
parents, who had originally provided the purchase monies. Mrs. Schwalm'
s
evidence
about the Boca Raton sale and the
proceeds differs in some respects. There is no documentation.

[
120
]

An earlier transaction was mentioned in respect of the family
residence that enhanced the position of the Trust. A mortgage was given to the
Trust on the family home at Breanna Court.

[
121
]

From the evidence, there have been various dealings in property, as
mentioned above, which have related to the Schwalms and to their family
interest, including the Trust, but have been carried out in such a way that the
benefit has been enjoyed not by the Schwalms but by others, without material
documentation. These dealings provide cause for further enquiry.

[
122
]

Counsel for the petitioner points out correctly that when it served
her purpose Mrs. Schwalm was able to produce detailed documentation of business
matters, in contrast to her evidence as to the dealings in respect of the
Trust. This adds to the impression that Mrs. Schwalm's evidence
is not reliable. Mr. Schwalm's evidence was not of
assistance in developing a reliable view of these matters.

The Baycrest debt; other obligations of
Mrs. Schwalm

[
123
]

Evidence was given that a debt in the amount of at least $157,000 is
outstanding and owed by Mrs. Schwalm to Baycrest Home for the Aged on account
of care for her parents. Counsel for the debtors said that the court ought not
to accept the document that Mrs. Schwalm signed with Mrs. Fairbloom of Baycrest
without an opportunity to cross-examine Mrs. Fairbloom about the circumstances
of the signing of the document. However counsel did not advance an argument
that, on the evidence now before the court, the document ought not to be
considered to reflect a binding obligation, so no basis is established as to
why the petitioner should have had the onus to call Mrs. Fairbloom. On Mrs.
Schwalm's judgment debtor examination as to her assets and liabilities, she
acknowledged Baycrest as a creditor. So there is no good reason not to accept
the evidence as to the indebtedness owed by Mrs. Schwalm to Baycrest.

[
124
]

Counsel for the petitioner submits that Mrs. Schwalm has also
admitted a liability to the Toronto-Dominion Bank and the Canadian Imperial
Bank of Commerce for her guarantees of small business loans and outstanding
credit card debt totalling about $50,000 plus outstanding property tax on her
home of about $11,000 and a debt of Revenue Canada of $13,000 on a
reassessment. Counsel for Mrs. Schwalm did not make any submission to the
contrary.

The Petition against William Schwalm

[
125
]

The outstanding judgment debts of Mr. Schwalm to Firehall suppliers
are referred to above. Mr. Schwalm also has outstanding indebtedness under a
judgment for unpaid personal income taxes under which about $56,000 is still
owing.

[
126
]

Mr.
Schwalm also has an outstanding judgment debt in favour of the
Ministry of Finance for Retail Sales Tax obligations of $157,838.99.

[
127
]

Counsel for the
debtors alluded to the fact that Mr. Schwalm had agreed to have his CPP and Old
Age Pension applied against his income tax debt rather than file for bankruptcy
because of the embarrassment personal bankruptcy would involve for him. There
was evidence from Mr. Schwalm about his concern in this regard, relating to
work that he does with charitable organizations.

[
128
]

Mr. Schwalm's
evidence in chief would suggest that he has little knowledge about the Schwalm
Family Trust and the affairs of the Firehall. However, Mr. Schwalm was a
trustee of the Family Trust until just before the hearing of the petition and
he has done tax returns for the Trust and the suggestion that he has little
relevant information is not persuasive. As the husband of Mrs. Schwalm, and a
member of the Schwalm family and a sometime trustee of the Family trust and a
preparer of tax returns for it, Mr. Schwalm may well have relevant information
about the Trust and its dealings and may have, or have had in the past, an
interest in the Trust, all of which is an appropriate area for further enquiry
and possible action about possible recoveries with respect to his outstanding
indebtedness.

[
129
]

Accordingly it is
in order that the receiving order should apply to him as well as to Mrs.
Schwalm.

Conclusion

[
130
]

For purposes of
s.
43(7)
of the
Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act
,
on the basis of the reasons
given above, this Court is not satisfied, with respect to either of Mr. and
Mrs. Schwalm, that they are able to pay their respective debts referred to
above and the Court does not find any sufficient cause why no order against
either of them should be made. Accordingly a receiving order is to go against
each of the debtors as requested by the petitioning creditor.

[
131
]

Counsel may speak
to me about costs.

Petition
granted.
